sub: Named after al-fatḥ, the “clear victory” (literally “opening”) in ayah 1
theme: The truce of al-Ḥudaybiyah looked like a defeat, but Allah calls it a clear victory. The surah praises those who pledged under the tree, exposes those who stayed behind, and promises the dream of entering Makkah will come true.
story: Revealed in 6 AH, on the way back to Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ had dreamt that he and his companions entered Makkah and performed ʿumrah. About 1,400 set out in iḥrām, driving sacrificial camels, carrying only sheathed swords, as pilgrims were allowed.

Quraysh blocked them at al-Ḥudaybiyah, on the edge of the sacred land. After the pledge under the tree, a truce was agreed: no war for ten years, go home now and return next year, and Makkans who fled to the Muslims would be sent back.

The terms felt humiliating. ʿUmar asked, “Why accept humiliation in our religion?” On the road home this surah came, calling the truce a clear victory. The Prophet ﷺ said it was dearer to him than the whole world. Soon Khaybar fell, and within two years Makkah was conquered.

sections.title: A clear victory: believers rewarded, hypocrites punished, the pledge made to Allah
sections.meaning: Allah calls the truce a clear victory. Through it He forgives the Prophet ﷺ, completes His favour, guides him and helps him. He sent calm into the believers’ hearts so their faith grew, promises them Paradise, and punishes the hypocrites and idolaters who expected disaster. Pledging to the Prophet ﷺ is pledging to Allah.
points: A clear victory: forgiveness, completed favour, guidance and mighty help
Calm sent into believers’ hearts; faith grows; gardens promised
Hypocrites and idolaters who thought evil of Allah are punished
The Prophet ﷺ is a witness, a bringer of good news, a warner
Pledging to you is pledging to Allah; His hand is over theirs
sections.matters: It turns the companions’ grief around at once. A deal that felt humiliating is declared a clear victory, and each group’s outcome is spelled out. It also gives the pledge its weight: a promise to the Prophet ﷺ is a promise to Allah.
sections.story: Revealed on the road home from al-Ḥudaybiyah, while the companions grieved over the truce. When the first ayat came, they said: “Congratulations to you, but what is there for us?” The promise of gardens (5) came in reply. Ayah 10 is about the pledge under the tree.
explained: Fatḥ means opening. The truce opened what had been shut: war stopped, people mixed freely, and crowds entered Islam. Through it Allah forgives the Prophet ﷺ his past and future faults, completes His favour, keeps him on the straight path and gives him help full of honour.

The companions swallowed hard terms, so Allah sent sakīnah into their hearts and their faith grew. He could win with His armies alone. Believers get gardens; hypocrites and idolaters, sure the Muslims would never come home, get His anger. So honour the Prophet ﷺ: a pledge to him is a pledge to Allah.
teaches: What looks like a loss can be the real victory.
Calm under pressure is a gift from Allah, and it grows faith.
Blessings should make us more grateful, not more relaxed.
Never think badly of Allah’s plan when things look bleak.
A promise made for Allah must be kept; breaking it only hurts you.
sections.hook: Ayat 2–3 list four gifts “for you”: forgive, complete favour, guide, help. “The armies of the heavens and earth” comes twice: 4 ends “Knowing, Wise”, 7 “Mighty, Wise”. The surah starts on page 511.

sections.title: The bedouins who stayed behind lie, lose the spoils, face another test
sections.meaning: The bedouins who stayed home make excuses and ask forgiveness they don’t mean. The truth: they expected the Muslims to be wiped out. When spoils are in sight they will want to come, but they are refused. Another test awaits them: a call to fight a mighty people. The blind, lame and sick are excused.
points: They claim they were busy and ask for forgiveness they don’t mean
They really expected the Muslims never to come home
A Blaze for deniers; Allah forgives or punishes as He wills
Refused the spoils: “Allah said so before.” They cry envy
A later call against a mighty people will test them
No blame on the blind, the lame or the sick
sections.matters: It shows how hypocrisy talks: busy with family, eager for gains, quick to cry envy. Yet the door stays open with a future test, and real excuses are accepted. Only the false excuse is rejected.
sections.story: When the Prophet ﷺ set out for ʿumrah, he called the tribes around Madinah to join him. Many stayed home, saying the Muslims were walking into death. Afterwards, the spoils of Khaybar were kept for those who had been at al-Ḥudaybiyah, and these bedouins asked to come.
explained: Al-mukhallafūn, “those left behind”, will say their wealth and families kept them busy, and ask the Prophet ﷺ to seek forgiveness for them. Their tongues say what their hearts don’t. In fact they thought the believers would never return, and that thought looked good to them. They were a people būr: ruined.

When the believers head out for spoils, the same men will say, “Let us follow you.” They want to change Allah’s word, which gave those spoils to the people of al-Ḥudaybiyah, and they reply, “You envy us.” Still, they will be called to face a mighty people: obey and be rewarded. The blind, lame and sick are excused.
teaches: Excuses may fool people, but never Allah.
No one can shield you from what Allah decrees, so don’t dodge your duty.
Those who share the hardship earn the reward.
A real hardship is excused; an invented excuse is not.
Allah keeps the door of repentance open.
sections.hook: Al-mukhallafūn is named three times: “They will say” opens 11 and 15, and “Say” opens 16. Ayah 17 repeats ḥaraj, “blame”, three times: blind, lame, sick.

sections.title: Allah is pleased with the pledge under the tree; war held back
sections.meaning: Allah was pleased with those who pledged under the tree. He saw their sincerity, sent calm, and rewarded them with a near victory and spoils, with more to come. Had Makkah fought, it would have fled. Allah held both sides back because hidden believers lived there. Makkans showed blind pride; believers held to taqwā.
points: Allah pleased with the pledgers: calm, a near victory, many spoils
Some spoils hastened, more promised; enemy hands held back
Had they fought, they would have fled: Allah’s unchanging way
He held both sides back near Makkah
Unknown believers in Makkah were the reason for no battle
Their pride of ignorance; the believers’ calm and the word of taqwā
sections.matters: It records Allah’s pleasure with the people of the pledge, a lasting honour. And it answers the painful question: why no battle? The believers would have won, but Allah held them back to protect hidden Muslims in Makkah and people who would later believe.
sections.story: Quraysh held ʿUthmān in Makkah and a rumour spread that he was killed, so the companions pledged under a tree. Armed Makkans who attacked the camp were caught and freed. Quraysh refused to write “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful” or “Messenger of Allah” in the treaty.
explained: Under a samurah tree, about 1,400 pledged not to flee, some said to the death. Allah knew the truth in their hearts, and their distress at the terms, so He sent sakīnah and rewarded them with a near victory, Khaybar, and its spoils. Far more was promised, and Allah held back the enemy’s hands as a sign.

Had Quraysh fought, they would have fled; that is Allah’s unchanging way. He held both sides back near Makkah because believing men and women lived there unknown and could have been killed by mistake. Quraysh acted from the pride of ignorance; Allah gave the believers calm and bound them to lā ilāha illā Allāh.
teaches: Allah sees the sincerity in hearts and rewards it.
Holding back strength can be the wiser choice.
Protecting innocent lives outweighs a quick win.
Pride and tribal ego block the truth; calm and taqwā follow it.
sections.hook: Sakīnah comes down twice here, in 18 and 26, after ayah 4. “He withheld hands” appears in 20, then again in 24, where both sides’ hands are held back.

sections.title: Allah confirms the Prophet’s ﷺ dream; his companions grow like a crop
sections.meaning: Allah confirms the Prophet’s ﷺ dream: they will enter the Sacred Mosque safely, heads shaved or trimmed. The delay hid wisdom, and a near victory came first. The religion of truth will prevail. Muḥammad ﷺ is Allah’s Messenger, and his companions are firm, merciful and devoted, growing like a strong crop.
points: The dream is true: you will enter the Sacred Mosque, safe
Guidance and the religion of truth, to prevail over all religion
Muḥammad ﷺ and his companions: firm, merciful, bowing, prostrating
Their likeness in the Torah and the Gospel: a crop growing strong
sections.matters: It answers the last doubt: the dream wasn’t false, only not yet. Then the surah closes by naming Muḥammad ﷺ as the Messenger of Allah, the very words struck from the treaty, and describing the people who stood with him.
sections.story: The journey began with the Prophet’s ﷺ dream of entering Makkah for ʿumrah. When they turned back, some companions were shaken and the hypocrites mocked. But the dream set no year. The next year, 7 AH, they entered Makkah in peace and performed ʿumrah.
explained: The dream was true; it just named no year. “You will enter,” in shāʾ Allāh, safe, some heads shaved and some trimmed, fearing no one. It came true the next year. Allah knew the good in waiting, and first gave a near victory: either the truce itself or Khaybar.

He sent His Messenger with guidance and the true religion, to rise above all others. Then: Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah. His companions are firm against the disbelievers, merciful to each other, often bowing and prostrating, marked by it on their faces. In the Gospel they are a crop: first a shoot, then strong stalks.
teaches: Say in shāʾ Allāh about the future; even this promise used it.
A promise delayed is not a promise broken.
Be firm on principle, and merciful with fellow believers.
Constant prayer leaves its mark on a person.
Small beginnings can grow into something strong.
sections.hook: Ayah 27 ends with fatḥan qarībā, as 18 did; the surah opened with fatḥan mubīnā. Ayah 29 names Muḥammad ﷺ outright. The surah ends on page 515, where Al-Ḥujurāt begins.

groups.text: Allah gives the Prophet ﷺ a clear victory, forgives his faults, completes His favour, guides him and helps him mightily.
Allah sent calm into believers’ hearts to grow their faith, and promises them gardens forever with their sins wiped away.
Hypocrites and idolaters who thought evil of Allah face His anger and Hell. The armies of heaven and earth are His.
The Prophet ﷺ is a witness, bringer of good news and warner: so believe, honour him, and glorify Allah morning and evening.
Pledging to the Prophet ﷺ is pledging to Allah. Breaking it harms only yourself; keeping it brings a great reward.
The bedouins who stayed home offer false excuses; really, they expected the Muslims never to return.
Deniers face a blazing Fire. Allah owns everything, forgives or punishes as He wills, and is Forgiving, Merciful.
Eager for spoils, they ask to come but are refused by Allah’s word. They cry envy, understanding little.
They will be called against a mighty people as a test. The blind, the lame and the sick are excused.
Allah was pleased with those who pledged under the tree, sent them calm, and rewarded them with a near victory and spoils.
Allah hastened some spoils, promised many more, held enemy hands back, and has other gains in store.
Had the disbelievers fought, they would have fled: Allah’s unchanging way. He held both sides back near Makkah.
No battle, because unknown believers lived in Makkah and could have been killed. Had they been apart, the disbelievers would have been punished.
The disbelievers’ pride of ignorance met the believers’ calm, and Allah bound them to the word of taqwā.
Allah made the dream true: they will enter the Sacred Mosque safely, heads shaved or trimmed, after a near victory.
He sent His Messenger with guidance and the true religion, to prevail over all religion. Allah is enough as Witness.
Muḥammad ﷺ and his companions: firm, merciful, prayerful, marked by prostration, described in the Torah and Gospel, promised forgiveness and a great reward.

1.explain: Fatḥ literally means opening. This clear victory is, for most, the truce of al-Ḥudaybiyah, which opened the way to peace and to Islam spreading. Some took it as the conquest of Makkah or of Khaybar.
1.why: Revealed on the way back from al-Ḥudaybiyah, while the companions grieved. The Prophet ﷺ said a surah had come that was dearer to him than the whole world. Another report says it answered mockers of 46:9, “I do not know what will be done with me.”

2.explain: Allah forgives his past and future faults, meaning lapses measured against a prophet’s high rank, completes His favour and keeps him on the straight path. He still prayed until his feet swelled: “Shouldn’t I be a thankful servant?”

3.explain: Naṣran ʿazīzā: mighty help that brings honour, with no humiliation in it. Islam would grow strong and its enemies weak.

4.explain: Sakīnah: calm and steadiness. The companions bore hard terms without breaking, and their faith grew, since faith rises and falls. Allah owns the armies of heaven and earth; He could win without them, but His wisdom chose this way.

5.explain: Believing men and women enter gardens forever, and their bad deeds are wiped away: they gain what they hoped for and escape what they feared. That is the great success.
5.why: When ayah 2 came, the companions said: “Congratulations, O Messenger of Allah! Allah has made clear what He will do for you. What will He do for us?” This came in reply.

6.explain: The hypocrites of Madinah and the idolaters of Makkah thought evil of Allah: that He would not help Muḥammad ﷺ and the believers would be destroyed. The evil turn they hoped for falls on them instead.

7.explain: The armies line returns, now ending “Mighty, Wise”: Allah will support His own soldiers and humble His enemies, yet every step follows His wisdom.

8.explain: Shāhid: a witness over his community. Mubashshir: he brings good news of reward to those who obey. Nadhīr: he warns those who disobey.

9.explain: So believe in Allah and His Messenger, support and revere him (tuʿazzirūhu, tuwaqqirūhu), and glorify Allah morning and evening. The first two may refer to the Prophet ﷺ or to Allah; the glorifying is for Allah.

10.explain: The pledge under the tree was really made to Allah. “Allah’s hand is over their hands”: He was with them, hearing and seeing it. Break it and you only harm yourself; keep it and the reward is great.

11.explain: They claim their property and families kept them busy, and ask for forgiveness without meaning it. Say: if Allah wants harm or good for you, who can stop it? He knows what you do.
11.why: Setting out for ʿumrah, the Prophet ﷺ called the nearby bedouins, reportedly of Ghifār, Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Ashjaʿ and Aslam, in case Quraysh fought. Many held back, claiming to be busy. This came about them.

12.explain: The real reason: they thought the Muslims would be wiped out and never come home, and the thought looked good to them. Qawman būrā: a ruined people with no good in them.

13.explain: Anyone who does not truly believe in Allah and His Messenger, whatever he shows outwardly, faces saʿīr, a blazing Fire.

14.explain: All dominion is Allah’s. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and He is Forgiving, Merciful, so the door stays open for those who repent.

15.explain: When the believers set out for spoils, at Khaybar, the stay-behinds ask to come. They want to change Allah’s word: those spoils were promised to the people of al-Ḥudaybiyah. Crying envy shows how little they understand.

16.explain: They will be called against a people of great might: either Hawāzin and Thaqīf, Banū Ḥanīfah of al-Yamāmah, or Persia and Rome. Fight them, or they submit. Obey and be rewarded; turn away again and be punished.

17.explain: No blame on the blind, the lame or the sick for staying behind. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger enters gardens; whoever turns away faces a painful punishment.
17.why: When ayah 16 warned those who turn away, people with lasting disabilities asked: “What about us, O Messenger of Allah?” This ayah excused them.

18.explain: Allah was pleased with those who pledged under the tree, a samurah acacia, so it is called Bayʿat ar-Riḍwān, the pledge of pleasure. He knew their sincerity, sent calm, and rewarded them with a near victory: Khaybar.
18.why: The Prophet ﷺ sent ʿUthmān to tell Quraysh they had come only for ʿumrah. Quraysh held him, and word spread that he was killed. So the Prophet ﷺ took a pledge under the tree: not to flee, or, in other reports, to fight to the death.

19.explain: And many spoils to take: the wealth and lands of Khaybar, shared among those who had been at al-Ḥudaybiyah. Allah could crush the disbelievers any time; in His wisdom He tests people through each other.

20.explain: Allah promises many spoils, every gain to the Last Day, and hastened this one: Khaybar, or the truce. He held back hands from you: either Quraysh at al-Ḥudaybiyah, or tribes who meant to raid your families in Madinah.

21.explain: And other gains not yet in your power, which Allah already has in His grasp: either Makkah, Persia and Rome, or every victory still to come. What He promises will surely happen.

22.explain: Had Quraysh fought you at al-Ḥudaybiyah, they would have turned and fled, finding no protector and no helper.

23.explain: Sunnat Allāh: His set way with nations before. When truth and falsehood truly clash, His soldiers win. That way never changes.

24.explain: He held their hands from you and yours from them bi-baṭni Makkah, near the heart of Makkah at al-Ḥudaybiyah, after He had given you the upper hand over them. He sees all you do.
24.why: Reportedly about eighty armed Makkans came down from at-Tanʿīm at dawn to attack the Prophet ﷺ and his companions. They were captured and set free, and this ayah came. Another report says thirty armed young men, caught while the treaty was being written.

25.explain: Quraysh barred you from the Sacred Mosque and kept the sacrificial camels from their place. But believers lived unknown among them; a battle could kill them by mistake, bringing maʿarrah: guilt or shame. Had they been apart, punishment would come.

26.explain: Ḥamiyyah: the proud rage of ignorance. They refused to write “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful” and “Messenger of Allah”. Allah gave the believers calm instead and bound them to kalimat at-taqwā, lā ilāha illā Allāh.

27.explain: The dream was true: you will enter the Sacred Mosque, in shāʾ Allāh, safe, heads shaved or hair trimmed, fearing no one. It happened the next year. Allah knew the good in waiting, and first gave a near victory.
27.why: When they turned back without ʿumrah, some companions were shaken and the hypocrites mocked that the dream was false. This ayah came: it will come true. The dream had named no year.

28.explain: Allah sent His Messenger with guidance, beneficial knowledge, and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over every religion. Allah is enough as Witness that he is truly His Messenger.

29.explain: Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah: the words Quraysh struck from the treaty, recited forever. His companions are firm against disbelievers, merciful among themselves, and often in prayer. Their sīmā, mark, is either light on their faces or humble bearing.
